newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Amnesty puts Nigeria in dock for rights abuses.
newsitem.headline: Amnesty puts Nigeria in dock for rights abuses.

text.p: Amnesty International said on Friday that Nigeria, which this week denied U.N. rights investigators access to detainees, was one of five states it was targeting for action at the 50th U.N. Human Rights Commission annual meeting next month.
The London-based human rights group identified four other states -- Colombia, Indonesia, Algeria and Turkey -- for close scrutiny at the meeting which opens on March 10.

Amnesty called on Nigeria in a statement to implement urgently a far-reaching programme of human rights reform, review all convictions of political prisoners, end torture and release unconditionally all political prisoners and rights activists.
"The present military government in Nigeria has a record of open contempt for human rights," said the statement issued in Geneva.
Two human rights investigators who were denied access to detainees by Nigeria this week said in a report issued on Friday they deeply regretted having had to cancel their fact-finding mission.

Malaysian lawyer Param Cumaraswamy, U.N. rapporteur on the independence of judges and lawyers, and Senegal's Bacre Waly Ndiaye, rapporteur on extrajudicial or arbitrary executions, insisted that full access to detainees was necessary.

Amnesty said: "This year Amnesty International is calling on the Commission to act in particular on five country situations where there is a pattern of persistent, severe and systematic violations of human rights.

"The fact that Amnesty International will be campaigning on these five countries does not mean the organisation will ignore other countries where there are gross violations of human rights," it added.

China, which last March successfully defeated a critical resolution at the U.N. Human Rights Commission for the fifth successive year, is also expected to come under fire from Western states, according to U.N. sources. Iran, Iraq and Israel are among other countries facing serious perennial rights allegations.
Indonesia, one of the four countries targeted by Amnesty, has come under fierce international criticism for its 1975 invasion and subsequent annexation of East Timor.

The U.N. Human Rights Commission last April unanimously adopted a resolution expressing deep concern about the situation in Nigeria following the November 1995 execution of author Ken Sara-Wiwa and eight Ogoni activitists. It called on Lagos to allow the two U.N. investigators to make a joint visit.

"The authorities continue to resort to arbitrary detention of prisoners of conscience; political prisoners continue to face the prospect of unfair trials by special tribunals which have the power to impose the death penalty; detainees continue to be denied access to lawyers, families and essential medical treatment; there continue to be allegations of extrajudicial executions by Nigerian law enforcement officials and torture and ill-treatment is widespread," Amnesty's statement said.

Nigeria drew outrage in November 1995 when it hanged Saro-Wiwa and eight Ogoni minority rights activists after their conviction in the 1994 murder of four pro-government tribal chiefs. Their trial was judged unfair by international judicial experts but they were denied the right to appeal.
The U.N. investigators were seeking to meet 19 jailed Ogoni leaders in Port Harcourt, linked to Saro-Wiwa, who also face the death penalty on the same murder charges.

The government was prepared to grant the U.N. investigators access to the detained Ogonis, but it denied access to other detainees either convicted by special tribunals or remanded on court order, according to a U.N. statement on Wednesday.
They included Moshood Abiola, presidential claimant jailed on charges of treason since June 1994, General Olusegan Obasanjo, Major-General Shehu Musa Yar'Adua and Beko Ransome-Kuti.
"Now you can expect Nigeria to be beaten up in the Commission," a U.N. source told Reuters.
